speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Private Security Industry Act (PSIA) provides for the regulation of private investigators, private investigation agencies, security officers, security agencies and security service providers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: It was introduced in 2007, with the aim of upgrading professional standards in the private security industry.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This was to enable the industry to better contribute to Singapore’s overall safety and security, as the security landscape evolves.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Since then, MHA and the Singapore Police Force (SPF) have continued to work closely with the industry on various initiatives to uplift industry standards.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: One example is the Security Industry Transformation Map (ITM) that was launched in 2018, which aims to shift the industry towards integrating skilled manpower and technology to deliver higher quality security services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Security officers are vital partners of the Home Team.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: They play important roles in safeguarding Singapore’s safety and security.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: They are deployed for important duties such as screening, security patrols and access control at a wide range of premises, both in the private and public.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In recent times, they have also stepped up to assist with COVID-19 safe management measures.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: These roles require them to interact with members of the public.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: While the large majority of the public are cooperative, there have been cases of persons confronting security officers carrying out their duties, with some going further to verbally or even physically abuse them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In 2019, a security officer at Roxy Square was verbally abused and punched by a man; a video that captured the incident was circulated widely.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Last year, a woman deliberately sneezed at a security officer at Ion Orchard, after she was denied entry for not wearing a mask.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: MHA has repeatedly emphasised that we take a very serious view of the abuse of security officers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Members of this House, the security industry and the union, have also called for better protection for security officers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Hence, the imperative to enhance the protection for security officers is clear and present.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Bill will also update the regulatory regime for certain security services, taking into consideration the development of the industry.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Section 17A of clause 3 creates an offence of assaulting or using criminal force to deter a security officer from discharging his or her duties.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Section 17B of clause 3 creates an offence of voluntarily causing hurt to a security officer in relation to the discharge of his or her duties.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: These offences take reference from similar offences under the Penal Code and carry harsher penalties compared to similar acts committed against general member of the public.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Section 17C of clause 3 creates an offence of intentionally causing harassment, alarm or distress to a security officer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: And this takes reference from similar offences under the Protection from Harassment Act (POHA) and the penalties are similar to harassment offences committed against public service workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Taking reference from POHA, section 17D of clause 3 provides for enhanced penalties for repeat offenders who have previously committed harassment offences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clause 7 amends POHA accordingly, so that the PSIA harassment offence will also be considered a precedent for enhanced penalties in relation to the relevant POHA offences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This ensures that there is consistency in the treatment of harassment offences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Section 17F of clause 3 provides that the civil remedies available to public service workers under POHA, such as Protection Orders, are also available to victims of the PSIA harassment offence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clause 5 provides that the new PSIA offences are non-arrestable, unless committed in the view of a Police officer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This takes reference from similar offences under POHA and the Penal Code.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: I will now speak about the second objective, on changes to the regulation of security services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Under the PSIA, persons who engage in the business of providing security services must be licensed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This includes security consultants who identify and analyse security risks and provide solutions or strategies to minimise these risks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: They also provide advice in relation to equipment designed to provide or enhance security, or for the protection or watching of any property; and they also provide services on security methods or principles, such as on preventing intrusion.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In January 2020, the Association of Certified Security Agencies (ACSA) and Security Association Singapore (SAS) launched the Security Consultants Accreditation Programme (SCAP) to develop competent security consultants with the requisite skills and competencies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The programme requires accredited security consultants to undertake continuous professional development and also has a disciplinary framework for infractions committed by the members.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: SPF has also worked closely with Temasek Polytechnic’s Security Industry Institute to develop a Specialist Diploma in Security Consultancy for security consultants to get formal certification of their role.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: There has also been no reported case of such abuse in the past five years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Even as we move towards industry oversight, if security consultants abuse sensitive information obtained in the course of their work to commit crimes, they would be prosecuted under other applicable laws.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Persons who provide any other security services that fall under section 18 of the PSIA, such as the sale, import, export, installation or maintenance of security equipment, will continue to be licensed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mdm Deputy Speaker, Singapore is one of the safest countries in the world.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Security officers are important partners of the Home Team in ensuring the safety and security of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Three weeks ago, I tabled the Private Security Industry (Amendment) Bill for the First Reading.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Singapore has a stringent licensing framework to regulate the security industry.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: All security officers must undergo and pass assessment for mandatory courses in order to be licensed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This ensures that they remain calm and are able to maintain public order and safety during an incident.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: However, security officers are often harassed by unreasonable members of public and sometimes verbally and physically abused.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Security officers are just performing their duties to enforce rules or regulations of the premises they protect.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Would we prefer the security officers to be irresponsible and not carry out their duties?

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Security officers are often caught in a bind – they are sometimes scolded when discharging their duties too firmly and also scolded when they are not.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In moving this Bill, we want to remind everyone to respect and protect the interests of security officers and deter abuse.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We often say we should not do unto others what we do not want done unto us.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: I appeal for everyone to continue to work with the industry and union to raise industry standards, and respect and recognise the important role played by security officers in ensuring we continue to enjoy living in a safe and secure Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: (In English): Mdm Deputy Speaker, security officers are important partners who support the Home Team’s efforts in keeping Singapore safe and secure.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The nature of their work puts them at higher risk of confrontation and it is necessary to ensure that they are adequately protected under the law.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for Minister for Home Affairs)
text: It is also necessary to update our regulatory regime for security services, to keep up with industry developments.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In our civil society, we should not tolerate anyone using abusive language, assault or cause hurt to another person, let alone using abusive language, assault and cause hurt to a security officer on duty.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Thus, it is timely for the Private Security Industry Act to be amended to make it an offence to abuse, assault or cause hurt to a security officer.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: With this newfound protection and power, if the Bill is passed, people will expect more from the security officer.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: (In Mandarin):   There are close to 50,000 security officers in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: They are of varying standards because of the low entry requirements.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In the past, security officers earned less than $1,000 a month and had to work 12 hours a day to just earn a living.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Fortunately, there has been an improvement in the salaries of security officers after the implementation of Progressive Wage Model in the security industry.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In 2019, there was a case of a senior executive in the finance sector that insulted a security guard at the car park of a condominium and sparked a public outrage.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This incident of abusing a security officer also shows the importance of amending the Private Security Industry Act.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The Private Security industry (Amendment) Bill aims to better protect our security officers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: With the new protections and powers, we need to ensure that security officers do not abuse their power to bully innocent people.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Recently, online shopping and food delivery have become a trend.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: There were cases where delivery persons were bullied by security officers when they delivered parcel or food to offices and condominiums.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Thus, I would like to ask the Minister of State three questions.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In other words, as long as security officers feel that they have been verbally abused by the other party and the other party is charged in Court, the chances of the other party being found guilty are much higher than in ordinary cases.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: It appears that the security officers are even better protected in this aspect than civil servants.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Thirdly, with the new protection measures, security officers may become more effective in their work.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: However, some black sheep may abuse their power and make life difficult for others for no good reason.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: At present, when people encounter an unreasonable security officer, they usually complain to the security company or the entity that hires their service.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Under the new framework, can the Minister consider allowing people to also lodge complaints with the Police Licensing and Regulatory Department?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If there are too many complaints, perhaps the relevant authority could consider setting up a separate department to investigate complaints.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Although I agree with the Bill to give more protection to our security officers, we also need to be aware of the counter effect of the amendments.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: (In English): Mdm Deputy Speaker, I agree with the additional protection to be given to the security officers with the amendments to the Private Security Industry Act.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: However, we need to better train the security officers so that they can understand the new clauses that protect them and not to abuse the new protective measures.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In addition, I have reservation why we need to shift the burden of proof from the prosecutor to the defence lawyer or the accused to prove, on a balance of probabilities, that the accused's conduct was reasonable under section 17(C)(3).

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The accused here refers to a person being accused to cause harassment, alarm or distress to a security officer.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If so, would the Police be more inclined to charge a person in Court when the person is accused to cause harassment, alarm or distress to a security officer because of section 17C(3)?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Would the Minister of State be able to explain the rationale of shifting the burden of proof from the prosecution to the defence?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: But we need to have sufficient safeguards against possible abuse so that the pendulum will not shift too much to the other direction.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: With increased concerns over the threat of terrorism and social frictions, such as race relations, the demands on our security sector are increasingly complex and challenging.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Yet, unfortunately, some negative stereotypes persist about private security officers among sections of our population.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Unarmed security officers are often labelled as "old and frail", or as "moonlighters sleeping on the job".

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Even their cousins, the auxiliary policemen, are derided as merely "acting like policemen" but having no real power to arrest, belying the police powers they are actually vested with.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They also signal the standing in which the private security profession ought to be held by the general public, which is crucial in attracting more capable talent, and upgrading and transforming the industry.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: As Members of Parliament working to help place our residents in jobs, we know that the private security industry is one sector which seems to have a constant demand for manpower.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This suggests that the turnover rate is high.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I urge MHA to continue to work on initiatives to attract, develop and retain capable young people into the industry and to keep advocating for their career development and empowerment.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: On the shift from licensing to industry-led accreditation for security consultants, I believe this could help to make the industry more competitive and grow the pool of competent security consultants.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Being industry-led, a well-run accreditation programme would also allow the industry to be more agile and responsive to changing needs and client demands.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It can also help to more clearly and objectively articulate the different skills, knowledge and experience required in different situations, paving the way for more recognition of these skills and, along with that, commensurate increase in wages and more sustainable remuneration packages which, again, can help to entice good people into the security industry.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The level of understanding and appreciation by buyers of the importance of higher quality services under certain circumstances is also a factor.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Faced with tenders going for the lowest bids, security companies may adopt different standards.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In an industry like security, standards and adherence to security protocols are so important, and varying practices and standards can be quite visible to the general public, which will only invite comparison.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I would, therefore, like to seek a few clarifications from the Minister of State.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Two, how can MHA encourage the industry to go for accreditation?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For example, by requiring accreditation to receive Government grants, or limiting providers for Government contracts to accredited companies or individuals.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What will be done to educate or require buyers of security services to require, and thereafter to fairly assess and compensate, security companies to have accredited security consultants where required?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Ultimately, it is important that the general public believes that the SCAP is acting in the interests of the public at large rather than in its own interests or the interests of its peers.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: (In Malay):   The private security industry hires a relatively high share of our Malay community.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I welcome the move to better protect security officers from harassment and abuse at work.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I also hope that it will signal to the public that they should give the private security profession due respect and the standing it deserves.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This is crucial in attracting more capable talent and upgrading the industry.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: A well-run industry accreditation programme for certain aspects of security services, could allow the industry to be more agile and responsive to changing client needs and demands.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This will also help to articulate the different skills, knowledge and experience required, thus paving the way for more recognition of these skills and, along with it, an increase in wages and remuneration packages that are more appropriate for security officers.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I urge that their accreditation requirements should include professional development.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I hope that these moves will open up more opportunities for young and capable Malays to develop their careers in this sector.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While they are tasked to protect property and persons, they are not adequately protected by the law in executing their duties.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: They are at risk when confronting hostile members of the public and can be unfairly targeted for simply carrying out the instructions of premise owners, instructions which could be unpopular or badly thought-through.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The diverse profile of security officers in the industry, ranging from the young to the elderly, is an added concern.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In 2019, the Government pushed ahead to raise standards of conduct among security officers by introducing a change to the Private Security Industry (Conduct) Regulations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While I understood the rationale behind the change, I raised concerns in Parliament at that time.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I was concerned about whether a strict implementation of the legislation would be fair, given the diverse profiles of security officers and varying resources available to them at their deployment sites.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: By enacting these specific offences, a public signal is being sent that conduct such as obstructing, abusing or harassing security officers are serious offences that will be punished accordingly.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I believe this is an appropriate approach for the offences of using criminal force and voluntarily causing hurt to security officers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, Madam, in order to ensure that this law will indeed improve outcomes for the industry and for the public, it must be accompanied by appropriate levels of training and the ability to attract able persons into the sector.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For the last few decades, there has been much outsourcing of work previously done by the Police to the Auxiliary Police and to private security.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Today, security officers are expected to do much more than just guard the entrances of factories or shopping malls in a balmy environment.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Today, security officers may be deployed to work in higher intensity conditions such as event security, crowd control and even to assist in search of persons.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier, the Minister of State also mentioned that they are deployed in enforcing COVID-19-related safe management measures, with high interactions with the public.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If they do not have adequate training, or their working environment is not conducive, altercations between them and the public are quite likely to take place.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To this end, I would stress that it is not just the hard skills that are required, for example, knowing what the laws are or the extent of a security officer's powers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is equally necessary that security officers have training in soft skills, to be able to handle difficult people, use tactful language and so on.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To take an example, security officers in shopping malls may actually spend more time on their shifts dealing with public enquiries about where certain facilities like toilets are located, rather than with the prevention of crime.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At the same time, being able to attract able persons to join the industry has not been easy.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: From my observations, there is a heavy reliance on Malaysians to fill security positions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In my former capacity as a Polytechnic lecturer, I had conducted some research into perceptions of Singaporean security officers on their work prospects.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At that time, about 15 years ago, some security officers told me that they will not encourage their children to enter the industry, mainly due to the long hours involved.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To this end, I note that the situation has improved somewhat.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In answer to my Parliamentary Question in July this year, MOM reiterated that the overtime hours for security officers have come down, even if the proportion of full-time security officers who still did overtime each month for last year was still nearly eight out of 10 officers, or 80%.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To attract able people to join the industry, the current efforts to improve the image and working conditions should continue.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier, the Minister of State mentioned the Security Industry Transformation Map (ITM) announced in 2018.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This ITM has identified key strategies which I agree have the potential to enhance the industry's image and capabilities.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, the concerted push towards adopting technology in operations has the potential to both improve job satisfaction and productivity, as well as to reduce manpower needs and long working hours for security officers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, I have observed instances of long and angry queues at the condominiums' entrances when new security systems are installed, with the security officers being the subject of verbal abuse.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On this front, I would urge managers of premises to work with security providers to ensure smooth rollouts of new systems and thereby to minimise stress on security officers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There are two main features of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, I would like to share some of USE's findings and efforts regarding the protection of our security officers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: No one would disagree that security officers' work is difficult: long hours, physically demanding, mentally challenging, uncomfortably juggling between protecting a site and providing quality customer service.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Now, they also help in enforcing safe management measures.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, some people see them as an inconvenient presence to bear with at best.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: USE commissioned SUSS to conduct a series of surveys from 2020, the most recent being in September and November of 2020.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This increase has been attributed to security officers enforcing safe management measures (SMMs).

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And, unfortunately, this seems to be their burden for some time to come.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need to stand by our security officers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They need our respect and they need our protection.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have come a very long way from calling them "jagas" and "guards" and now, rightfully, "security officers".

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They are critical to combating the spread of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Progressive Wage Model (PWM) has given them their rightful standing in the security landscape.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Now, we need to do more for them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: USE and MHA have been the vanguard in protecting our security officers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In clear cases of abuse of security officers, USE assists security officers in lodging Police reports.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Because our older security officers may not be aware of their rights.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must also help to mediate disputes and steer away from litigation as much as possible.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: USE launched its Mediation Services in 2018 to resolve issues and disputes involving security officers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In recent years, the Services has seen a marked increase in cases.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In a recent case, an officer was tasked with managing entry into a club's facilities room.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: A visitor, apparently upset with the verification process, vented his frustration and dragged the officer from the chair.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The matter was reported to the union and investigations are ongoing.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But there should not be such disrespect in the first place.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must reinforce this protection of our officers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need enhanced penalties against abusers of security officers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is even more urgent now during COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Abusers must not breach our defence of SMMs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, it seems that we can only prove liability if the offence is committed while the security officer is doing his duty.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What if an abuser abuses and threatens an officer while the latter is off duty because of an earlier incident?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Second, the elements of section 17C is substantively in pari materia to section 3(1)(a) and (b) of the Protection from Harassment Act (POHA).

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, section 3(1)(c) of the POHA, which relates to the offence of doxxing, is not found within the proposed section 17C.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Abusers can use social media to publish personal information to harass these officers and their families.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could the Ministry consider including the offence of doxxing in section 3(1)(c) of POHA within the proposed section 17C?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Next, will the Ministry consider the inclusion of section 5 of POHA within the amendments as well?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This section concerns causing fear, provocation or the facilitation of violence.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Like section 3 of POHA, section 5 also relates to abusive behaviour which security officers may face during their course of duty.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Next, I would like to speak on the proposed shift to accredit security consultants by the industry.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The security consultants must take Continuous Professional Development under the Security Consultants Accreditation Programme (SCAP).

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They are subject to the yearly renewal of their accreditation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This pivot ensures that Security Consultants are attuned to the new security trends and needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These consultants can help guide service buyers on outcome-based security contracts as qualified persons by leveraging technology rather than manpower.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This makes wage increases in the security PWM sustainable.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Better jobs and better pay for the longer run.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mdm Deputy Speaker, this Bill enhances the protection of our security officers and improves their working environment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Security officers are our frontline workers who have tirelessly kept Singapore safe and protected.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The amendment Bill will ensure that our officers can carry out their duties without the fear of repercussions and impose harsher punishments on abusers of our security officers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Quite often, our security officers also face unfriendly behaviours and attitude from the public.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I urge that we must all stand up against such disrespect of security officers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Besides their employers, we are all entrusted to preserving respect for our security officers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: (In English): Mdm Deputy Speaker, this Bill enhances the protection of our security officers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Security officers are our frontline workers who have tirelessly kept Singapore safe and protected.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But we are all entrusted to preserving respect for our essential workers.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For instance, the Progressive Wage Model developed by the Security Tripartite Cluster implemented in 2016 helped to encourage security officers to upgrade their skills and achieve productivity-based wage progression.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Taken collectively, these measures have certainly benefited the security industry.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In recent years, several high-profile incidences of security officers being physically and verbally abused by members of the public have been reported in the media.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In September 2019, as mentioned in Minister of State Desmond's speech, a man was jailed for punching a security officer at Roxy Square.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In January 2021, another man was jailed for punching a security officer after breaking through a safe distancing barricade and causing a ruckus at Jurong Point.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And in a video that went viral on social media, a member of the public was recorded to be berating an elderly security officer and using insulting language on him when the security officer informed him that he needed to pay a fee for his friend to park his vehicle in a condominium after 11 pm.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These are all examples of utterly reprehensible behaviour towards our security officers.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As such, the proposed amendments to the Private Security Industry Bill are timely and important.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is heartening to know that the amendments to the Bill will strengthen the penalties against verbally and physically abusing security officers.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has impacted everyone, especially frontliners like healthcare workers and security officers.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Not only do these workers need to carry out their daily duties, they also find themselves having to interact more frequently with members of the public than before the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Part of the increase in incidence of abuse could be attributed to possible tensions that arise from the implementation of COVID-19 related measures, such as safe entry and safe management measures.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While it is understandable that the public might be frustrated by COVID-19-related measures and are even confused in the initial stages when regulated entries into premises are managed and regulated, these frustrations and confusions should not be vented on security officers who are doing their job.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The amount of psychological stress experienced by security officers is arguably higher than that of the public as they are now required to take on new responsibilities beyond just security work.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They certainly should not be subjected to additional emotional stress of having to deal with this verbal abuse.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Not only do we need to safeguard and protect our security officers from abuse and harassment, but we also need to take care of their mental and emotional wellness too.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that the Government will consider implementing an industry-wide Employee Assistance Programme (EAP) for security officers.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Companies that have implemented EAPs have found them to be effective in promoting mental and physical well-being of their employees.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Positive impacts of EAPs include lowered absenteeism and turnover, improved well-being and productivity.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The EAP for the security industry can be a permanent feature spearheaded by the industry association and union to provide an additional layer of support for security officers.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Most companies have chosen to outsource their security services to providers, others continue to hire their security officers directly as their employees to maintain stronger control over the training and deployment of these officers.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The latter approach could possibly be adopted by public service organisations if these organisations wish to have stronger oversight over the provision of security services on their premises.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would this lead to a differentiated level of protection based on employers and employment arrangements?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If so, would the Government consider aligning the penalties to ensure parity for all security officers, regardless of the institution and organisation they are working for, and whether they are outsourced or direct-hire staff?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While this Bill has introduced additional protections for security officers from physical and verbal abuse, I would like to propose that we consider additional legislation to further enhance the working conditions of the security officers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I had spoken to security personnel in my constituency and they shared these concerns with me.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Similarly, members of the condominium management committees have highlighted and given similar feedback.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This COVID-19 pandemic has brought out the worst in many offenders because there are more regulations.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Security officers have more responsibilities today – new ones which did not exist before, such as ensuring that people wear their masks, maintain safe distancing and not exceed certain group sizes while on their properties.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some security personnel told me that there are residents or visitors who blatantly disregard the regulations, by gathering in big groups, pulling down their masks whilst walking, smoking and so on.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Attempts by the guards to advise them lead to altercations.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Security officers tell me that they have been totally ignored or verbally abused whilst the breaches continue to take place.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: MCSTs should also be accorded more powers to deal with such offenders on their estates.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: MCSTs should also be accorded more powers to deal with such offenders on their estates.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The private security sector should be treated as an important partner in our national security framework and their officers should be empowered to do their jobs well and effectively.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: When I first got to know about this Bill, I contacted my fellow Union leaders from USE and asked for their views about the changes that the Bill could bring for our workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I wanted to know if the amendments will improve the workers in the four key areas that we are concerned about: protection, progression, placement and privileges.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: These 4Ps are NTUC’s key pillars that every union leader is working towards in achieving, in addition to the 3Ws: wages, welfare and work prospects for our workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: USE leaders' immediate response to me was this, I quote, "Brother Samad, this Bill signifies that the Government never fails to hear our calls to improve the protection of our security officers in their course of work and we certainly welcome these amendments." For those who are not aware of USE and what they do, USE is one of 58 unions affiliated to NTUC.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Formed in 1978, they represent all persons who are employed in the security and security-related services.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: USE has evolved over the years and currently represents over 20,000 union members.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Security officers are aware that USE leaders are security officers, as well as workers from the industry.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: However, they take on the additional role by walking the ground and understanding the concerns and issues faced by the workers to better serve their needs.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond providing social benefits via NTUC Social Enterprises, USE actively carries out industrial relations works.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, they started USE Mediation Service in 2018 as unionised security agencies and union members felt that USE understood the industry practices and was in a better position to deal with grievances.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: On average, they have been handling over 200 cases per year.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The number of cases has been on the rise since COVID-19 struck us last year.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Last year, USE handled 267 cases, the same number of cases they see now year-to-date, and we still have one more quarter to go.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: USE Mediation Service serves not just members but all officers in the security industry by helping them to mediate issues that range from salary payment to harassment cases.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: USE will soon launch an app in the fourth quarter this year to allow officers and agencies to report any harassment or work-related grievances for Union to take action together with our tripartite partners.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This is in line with NTUC’s belief that Members First, Workers Always, which means every worker matters.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, USE recently has collaborated with the Singapore University of Social Sciences (SUSS) to conduct a longitudinal study to track changes in the wages, welfare and work prospects among security officers in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This is a 10% increase in a matter of months.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: A security officer was deployed at a condominium and shared that the tenant and condominium manager at the site had been constantly yelling at them, being disrespectful and using profanities at the security officers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: He brought up the issue to his Operations Executive on multiple occasions.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: However, no follow-up actions were taken by the security agency.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, the security officer sought help from, who and where else, USE Mediation Service.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Upon receiving the report, USE engaged the security agency and stressed that USE does not condone such behaviour towards any security officers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The agency acknowledged and assured that the matter will be addressed with the condominium manager.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This incident was investigated and the condominium manager was issued with a stern warning for his actions.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This is just one of the many cases that our union leaders have represented and protected the interest of our workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: It will give the security officer assurance towards any form of assault or criminal force, voluntarily hurt caused by members of the public and also against any indecent, threatening words or behaviour, or such communication against security officers, with intent to cause and as a result causing harassment, alarm or distress.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This is very welcoming and heartening news for all our security officers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: For example, USE has pointed out that some altercations could be avoided through the better deployment of technology and manpower in order to minimise in-person interactions with officers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This is also in line with NTUC’s push for workplace transformation and towards achieving worker 4.0.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: (In Malay):   The amendments to this Act have been long awaited by security officers who have frequently been challenged when carrying out their duties.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Please know that the Union of Security Employees (USE) will always be with you to listen to your grievances about your job and every feedback, and we will do our best to find the best solution for all of you.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Many of us know and have also heard stories of security officers being insulted, scolded or verbally abused when carrying out their duties.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, I would like to encourage all security officers to become union members and seek the USE's assistance.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: If you do not know anyone from USE, please visit the Mediation Centre located within Textile Centre which is at Jalan Sultan.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This centre provides a dedicated service for you.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: We will always listen to you and help you with any problems related to work and the workplace.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Do not just fill the pockets of your bosses.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This transformation came as a result of the efforts of USE and NTUC, to improve the capabilities of each officer so that they can reap better benefits in terms of their salary, welfare and career advancement.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: They are aware of these added responsibilities and they also hope to receive support from all parties in order to carry out their duties.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I call on all parties to appreciate every security officer, whose job is becoming increasingly challenging, especially during the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: To all security officers, I hope that this Act will make you feel safer in performing your duties.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Once again, I invite you to join the union so that you can reap its benefits and please visit the Mediation Centre for assistance if you encounter problems at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: (In English): Beyond this Bill, with the presence and continuous advocacy from USE, security officers are being better protected and we encourage more to join the union and allow us to represent and serve you.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: But as professionals, they do their jobs when called upon.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Behind every abuse is an officer who feels upset, angry and emotional, so, we appreciate these amendments in giving security officers greater protection.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: To all security officers, on behalf of NTUC and USE, I would like to convey my appreciation for the good work you do in keeping our loved ones safe.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Be assured that with USE and NTUC around, you will never walk alone and we will always be here for you.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In addition to their usual work, many now have to do the thankless task of enforcing COVID-19 safe management measures.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Union of Security Employees says that this has increased tensions for security officers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill is a welcome step for increased protection for them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, I would like to ask what counts as a security officer's duty.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill is meant to protect security officers from abuse.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To this end, it strongly punishes individuals for assaulting, hurting or harassing security officers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, this enhanced punishment kicks in only if it happens during the execution or discharge of duty by the officer.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to be clear about this as security officers may be required to perform diverse tasks not outlined in section 13 of the Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Such tasks may equally put the security officers at risk of abuse and harassment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should look to protect security officers performing such tasks too.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second clarification relates to the defences against the offence of intentionally causing harassment, alarm or distress to a security officer under section 17C.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Notably, the wording of section 17C tracks the wording used in section 3 of the Protection from Harassment Act (POHA).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Section 3 of POHA deals with the offence of intentionally causing harassment, alarm or distress.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One of the defences to section 17C is that the accused did not know or had no reason to believe that the words, behaviour or communications would be perceived by the target person.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, this is not a defence to the similar offence of intentionally causing harassment in section 3 of POHA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Instead, this defence appears only in section 4 of POHA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Section 4 of POHA deals with the offence of behaviour, which is likely to cause harassment, alarm or distress.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Importantly, section 4 is different from section 3 of POHA in that it does not require intention to cause harassment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It seems inconsistent that a defence to a harassment offence in POHA that does not require the element of intention now applies to a harassment offence in the Private Security Industry Act, which requires intention.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In addition to inconsistency across legislation, this seems difficult to understand in principle.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Surely, someone who acted with the intention to harass another person should not be allowed to say that they had no reason to believe that harassing conduct would not be perceived by the victim.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Does this suggest that intentional harassment under the Private Security Industry Act has a different scope from intentional harassment under POHA?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Security officers play an unsung but important role in our society.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We sleep soundly at night, knowing that with their vigilance, we are safe and that our property is protected.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Yet, security officers are not safe from abuse.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We cannot claim to be a gracious and kind society if our workers are going into work expecting that it is unfortunate but normal to be insulted, threatened or even assaulted on the job.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need to improve protection and welfare of our security officers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mdm Deputy Speaker, we must be able to deter harassment by ensuring effective means to capture concrete evidence.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Bill introduces definitions to the offences that constitute the types of harassment and abuse faced by security officers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, without a witness or closed-circuit camera in the vicinity, harassment and verbal abuse can be difficult to prove.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The high-profile case of a condominium resident verbally abusing a security guard last year came to light only because it was caught on video and then circulated.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many other security officers would suffer in silence.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Notwithstanding, we must account for the need to balance the provision of adequate protection with the challenges of ensuring data privacy, as well as managing rising costs in the industry.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To address these concerns, one suggestion is for body cameras to be considered if the security guard works in a location where he is susceptible to higher risks of abuse, patrolling alone or out of range of nearby closed-circuit television (CCTVs).

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The body camera proposal is not just beneficial for the wearer.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Section 17 of POHA states that the burden remains on the prosecution to prove the offence is beyond a reasonable doubt and disprove a defence raised based on a balance of probabilities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, whether the accused's choice of words and tone can be interpreted as abuse is subjective.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Moreover, prior provocation may have occurred to lead to their choice of words and tone.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There has been feedback that some security officers are rude.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There are usually two sides to every story.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The truth usually lies somewhere in the middle.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The body camera can help to even the odds.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It can shed some objective light into where truth may lie.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If harassment of security officers falls under this Act, the burden of proof falls on the accused to justify their word choice and behaviour.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Likewise, without witnesses and audio-visual proof, it will be difficult to prove their innocence.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Yet, in the eyes of the law, an accused is innocent until proven otherwise or beyond reasonable doubt.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The onus should be on the plaintiff, in this case, the security guard, to provide the evidence of harassment or abuse.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In this case, the evidence would come from the officer's body camera.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is indisputable evidence that is up for evaluation by the Court, rather than personal interpretation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mdm Deputy Speaker, security officers must be equipped with the necessary skills to protect themselves and to react appropriately when faced with aggression.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Self-defence training should be recommended and made accessible for those who are in the security industry or planning to join it.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These courses should be tailored to different age groups.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is because the age demographic in the industry is varied, with youngsters in their 20s to elderly in their 60s.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Those in a front-facing role should also receive training on communication skills.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These skills should focus on managing disputes with residents and de-escalating conflicts.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In this regard, would such training and skillsets be made mandatory in subsidiary legislations or guidelines?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How does the Government plan to work with the industry to further professionalise the sector and provide pathways for progression?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, these skillsets are transferable and will serve security officers well if they wish to explore other roles or to take on greater responsibilities in the sector.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mdm Deputy Speaker, security officers are often ordered to do things that are beyond their job scope and they rarely receive remuneration for it.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A resident of mine who is a security officer in a condominium told me that he has been asked to drop off the mail or food delivery, water the plants or even clean up messes when the cleaner is not available.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Whilst some security officers do so out of goodwill, it should not be a given.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Not only is this unfair, it is also dangerous.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They are called away from their focus of security work.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In the meantime, there is no one around to cover for them.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Although they can lodge a complaint to MOM, I have been informed that some employers tend to side with the residents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Lodging a complaint may also threaten the officer's job security, so most would rather accept the extra work.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But it takes more than laws to eradicate the undesirable mentality that such workers are at the beck and call of the privileged who engage their services.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must continue to address this problem through multiple angles.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This includes drawing awareness to the problem through education and by enforcing stiff penalties against those who abuse their positions of power towards the vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A few residents shared with me about their distresses with job hunting at my Meet-the-People Sessions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They were keen to be security officers, given the high demand for such jobs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This information is not immediately clear from the Security Officer Licence application website.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, past media reports suggest that this is indeed the case.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I recognise that the public and buyers of service may be uncomfortable with ex-offenders as private security guards, due to the perception that ex-offenders may recidivate.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Be that as it may, if the industry further evolves and develops sub-specialties in roles, surely we can find positions for ex-offenders in the industry.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These include appropriate roles that give them an opportunity to perform and show that they have reintegrated into society, without the perceived risk of putting a known thief to guard one's belongings.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: From there, they can further professionalise and assume greater responsibilities, having demonstrated that they have turned over a new leaf, perhaps through licensing and so on.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When a child goes missing in a mall, the parents would ask the security officer for help to look for the child.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When one encounters a stalker, they head immediately to the nearest security officer for protection.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is ironic that despite our reliance on security officers for safety, they command little respect and recognition for their work.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The Labour Movement welcomes the key amendments which will enhance the protection of security officers, as well as the shift towards the industry-led accreditation of security consultants.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: (In Malay):   During COVID-19, many security officers have stepped up to take on more tasks to ensure our well-being, including temperature-taking, crowd control and the checking of SafeEntry check-ins.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: These steps have been essential in helping our community curb the spread of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: However, these additional tasks have also meant that our security officers have increased interactions with the public, including those who may be hostile.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Recently, we have seen a few cases in the news of abuse towards security officers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This is worrying, and the Labour Movement condemns these acts of intimidation and abuse.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Abuse towards security officers may be more commonplace than we think.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The amendments to enhance the protection for security officers are thus timely.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: (In English): The second amendment, the shift towards the industry-led accreditation of security consultants is an important step for the private security industry.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: With this amendment, the certification of security consultants would now reside within the industry, which potentially signals an increased availability of qualified security consultants who can help buyers buy security correctly: conduct a proper security assessment, install the right technology and deploying ably trained manpower to leverage the technology.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This Assessment, Technology and Manpower or ATM approach can improve security outcomes significantly and lower overall security costs through increased productivity.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The ATM approach also complements outcome-based contracting, where clients specify outcomes rather than go by the traditional procurement method of specifying headcounts.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Outcome-based contracts also advocate for the use of technology and job redesign which can help to make the work of security officers more efficient and effective.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: With the use of technology such as the remote gate guarding, facial recognition, visitor management system and remote video surveillance, the service buyer has been able to achieve the same or better outcomes.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The transition to outcome-based contracting can be daunting for many service buyers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Many are unsure how to craft an outcome-based tender specifications that may be intimidated by the upfront cost of purchasing technology.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Furthermore, it can also prove challenging to convince all stakeholders that the transition to outcome-based contracting will be a fruitful one.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: For example, many residents in condominiums may still feel that having security officers on-site 24/7 is important.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: However, after undertaking the transition, the benefits often outweigh the initial adjustment period.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: One such example of a security agency that was able to help their clients better procure security services via outcome-based sourcing is Focus Security.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: In addition to increased productivity, a better-designed deployment plan coupled with technology adoption will help minimise the risk of abuse of security officers who will no longer need to manually enforce rules in a public-facing setting.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The proposed amendments will send a clear signal that any abuse will not be tolerated and enhance the pool of qualified security consultants who can help buyers better procure security services.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As a Labour Movement, we applaud these amendments and continue to work to improve wages, welfare and work conditions for security officers together with our tripartite partners.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As guardians of the premises where they are deployed, it is common for them to have to deal with difficult stakeholders who could have malicious intent, are uncooperative, or are just plain rude.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Members in this House may remember several high-profile cases of abuse towards security officers, such as in 2019, when a viral video emerged of an investment banker verbally abusing a security officer working in a condominium over a $10 parking fee for visitors.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has made the situation worse.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Although abuse of security officers may happen frequently, my sense is that the number of Police reports made against abusers are few and far between.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: And possibly only a tiny handful of abusive incidents ever translate into arrests and prosecutions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: One key issue is likely to be a lack of clear evidence.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: How can we get past the usual impasse of one person's word against the other?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: What can we do to enhance current procedures to make it easier for security officers to take abusers to task, especially considering the proposed new offences?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: These cameras have shown to be effective in breaking the deadlock, allowing organisations and individuals to report incidents with confidence.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Police introduced body-worn cameras for its frontline Police officers back in 2015.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: These cameras capture both audio and video, and are worn in a visible manner on the front of the officer's uniform.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The cameras can serve as a deterrent against potential abuse of our security officers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The footages can also serve as evidence for police reports to be made against the offender.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The lack of manpower has an impact on the safety of the premises that our security officers protect.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Overworked and tired officers may miss out on threats due to fatigue.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The lean workforce also means that security officers sometimes must patrol alone and may not be able to call for timely help if they are attacked.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I hope that the Ministry can review this without compromising on the stringent selection criteria for our security professionals.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While we make the timely legislative amendments to enhance the protection of our security officers, it is also important for us to consider other measures to improve the safety and well-being of our security professionals.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The ability to prosecute abusers is one crucial deterrent, but just as important is the ability to de-escalate situations before they become unacceptable or unlawful behaviour.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: At the outset, Madam, I would like to register my strong and wholehearted support for the Bill.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Second, it will no longer be required for security consultants to be licensed under the Act.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: By way of background to the first set of amendments, the security industry associations and union had lobbied MHA for some years to consider amending the Protection from Harassment Act (POHA) to include security officers in the definition of "public service officers".

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This had also been raised by Mr Patrick Tay in this House, as well as Mr Zainal Sapari.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, clearly the stakeholders were delighted when MHA suggested that we instead introduce protections for security officers under the PSIA.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Section 17D provides for circumstances where enhanced penalties may apply.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: What is significant is that the penalties prescribed in each section are higher than that stipulated for similar offences under the POHA.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This is an important recognition that it is particularly egregious to harass, or to assault or to hurt a security officer while he is carrying out his functions, because the role that he plays is essential and critical to the orderly functioning of society.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: To a certain extent, these provisions are a corollary to the amendments made to the Private Security Industry (Conduct) Regulations in 2019.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Those amendments introduced penalties, including fines and jail terms, for security officers caught being remiss in the conduct of their duties.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The rationale for those amendments was to hold security officers up to a high level of conduct, if they were remiss while on duty, precisely because of their critical functions.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It is, therefore, fair and fitting that even as we underscore with those amendments the importance of security officers’ duties, that we also move the current amendments to afford greater protections for them.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The urgency for these new provisions is apparent.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The Union of Security Employees (USE) and the Singapore University of Social Sciences (SUSS) conducted two surveys that had been referred to by several speakers today.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Older officers were found to face abuse on a more frequent basis.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The Minister of State mentioned in his speech the incident in 2019 where Mr Andrew Lim, a security supervisor at Roxy Square, was punched in the face by one Stuart Boyd Mills.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The sheer force of the punch knocked SS Andrew to the ground.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Mills was later convicted and sentenced to a week’s jail under POHA.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In another even more unfortunate incident, 74-year-old Security Officer Chew Choo Chian caught and reprimanded one Teo Chin Lai for urinating behind a door of a Bukit Panjang shopping centre.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Teo punched SO Chew in the chest and SO Chew fell backwards and suffered injury to his cervical spine.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Sadly, SO Chew died from his injuries six weeks later.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, causing grievous hurt as in this case is not part of the amendments to the PSIA, and will still fall under the Penal Code, but my point is that security officers, as frontline workers and as enforcers of rules, are often subject to physical abuse, which has caused injury and has even been fatal on occasion.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As regards incidents of verbal abuse and harassment, these are abundant and a simple search on Google will pull up numerous media articles, videos and accounts of such behaviour.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, I would like to say to all our security officers: your uniform, your PLRD ID are now symbols of the protection that you now have.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In the course of your duties, if you are verbally abused, if you are harassed, assaulted or hurt, you are now protected by law.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, carry out your duties proudly, responsibly, professionally and if you are subject to any form of abuse, report it and action will be taken.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: There are various ways for reporting to be done.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As these are now statutory offences, ultimately at some point, the abused officer will have to make a Police report.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Chief amongst these is the Progressive Wage Model that the Security Tripartite Cluster will announce soon.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Another important initiative was launched by Senior Minister of State Zaqy Mohamad in July this year: the Security Industry Workplace Safety and Health Guidelines, which was drafted by a committee co-chaired by SAS and USE.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Third, MOM also launched the Workcare Grant in May this year, which was mentioned by Members earlier.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: These initiatives go a long way to build workplaces and working conditions that are reasonable, fair and that empower officers to do their best at work.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
